newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM says trade gap not fixable in short term.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM says trade gap not fixable in short term.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus told parliament on Thursday it was impossible to reverse the ballooning trade deficit soon and declared that an "artificial" fix would be undesirable.

"It's not possible to change the deficit in the short term, and I am not even sure that to reach (a change) articificially would be a result which would be desirable in the short term," Klaus said during a parliamentary question and answer session.

Klaus, responding to a opposition question on what the government planned to do about a 1996 trade deficit which reached 100 billion crowns in the first eight months, said the exports were still growing faster than gross doemstic product (GDP).
He told parliament exports had grown "in real terms" by 6.4 percent in the January to August period, year-on-year.
The official Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) reported exports during the first eight months had grown 6.4 percent in nominal terms, while imports grew a nominal 15.2 percent.
Real inflation-adjusted GDP for the first half of the year grew 4.3 percent, year-on-year, according to the CSU.
Klaus said that the exports of agricultural goods were hampered by "frozen" markets in the west and the east.
He said exports of industrial consumer goods had grown by 19.1 percent this year, with machinery and transport equipment up 15.5 percent for the eight-month period, year-on-year.

Klaus however said the larger trade gap, which has led independent economists to forecast a current account deficit of between 5.5-6.0 percent of GDP in 1996 from four percent last year, was caused by investment into infrastructure and modernisation.
Opposition politicians have turned up the heat on the government recently to do something about the trade situation.
Some economists have suggested a devaluation of the Czech crown to boost exports, a measure repeatedly ruled out by Klaus's government and the central bank.

"I believe the development of our foreign trade is logical," Klaus said but added that those who want to change the current trade balance in effect want to lower the volume of investment in the Czech Republic.
He said that there were significant increases in funding for pro-export agencies like the Czech Export Bank and its sister export insurance agency EGAP.
